chunk_text: The 301 Moved Permanently status code indicates that the target resource has been assigned a new permanent URI. The response should include a Location header indicating the new URL. Any future references to this resource should use one of the returned URIs. Note that user agents may change the request method from POST to GET on subsequent redirection.

The 307 Temporary Redirect status code indicates that the target resource resides temporarily under a different URI. The user agent MUST NOT change the request method if it performs an automatic redirection to that URI: if a POST was used in the first request, a POST must be used in the redirect. The response must include a Location header.

The 400 Bad Request status code indicates that the server cannot or will not process the request due to something that is perceived to be a client error. Typical causes include malformed request syntax, invalid query parameters, deceptive request routing, or framing errors. The client should not repeat the request without modifications.

The 401 Unauthorized status indicates that the request has not been applied because it lacks valid authentication credentials for the target resource. The server generating a 401 response MUST send a WWW-Authenticate header field containing at least one challenge applicable to the target resource. Do not assume the token expired; check whether the header is present and uses the documented scheme.

The 403 Forbidden status code indicates that the server understands the request but refuses to authorize it. Unlike 401, re-authenticating with the same credentials will make no difference because the authenticated identity lacks necessary permissions, roles, or scopes to access the resource.

The 404 Not Found status code indicates that the origin server did not find a current representation for the target resource or is not willing to disclose that one exists. A 404 status does not by itself indicate whether the resource is temporarily missing, path casing differs, or the endpoint has been deleted; verify path segments and resource identifiers.

The 405 Method Not Allowed status code indicates that the request method is known by the server but is not supported by the target resource. The origin server MUST generate an Allow header field in a 405 response containing a list of the target resource's currently supported methods (for example: Allow: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS).

The 410 Gone status code indicates that access to the target resource is no longer available at the origin server and that this condition is likely to be permanent. Clients should cease sending requests to this URI. Unlike 404, 410 informs caches and clients that the resource was intentionally removed.

The 413 Payload Too Large status code indicates that the request entity is larger than limits defined by the server. The server may close the connection to prevent the client from continuing the request. Clients must reduce payload size, compress data, or chunk the upload into smaller segments.

The 415 Unsupported Media Type status code indicates that the origin server is refusing to service the request because the payload format is in an unsupported format. The inspection of Content-Type or Content-Encoding header determines media type compatibility. Verify that Content-Type is application/json when sending JSON payloads.

The 422 Unprocessable Content status code indicates that the server understands the content type of the request entity and the syntax is correct, but it was unable to process the contained instructions. Common causes include missing required fields (such as 'title'), semantic validation failures, or incorrect value data types.

The 429 Too Many Requests status code indicates the user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time (rate limiting). The response representations SHOULD include details explaining the condition, and MAY include a Retry-After header indicating how long to wait before making a new request in seconds.

The 500 Internal Server Error status code indicates that the server encountered an unexpected condition that prevented it from fulfilling the request. This is a generic server-side error response meaning something broke on the server itself, such as an unhandled exception or database failure.

The 502 Bad Gateway status code indicates that the server, while acting as a gateway or proxy, received an invalid response from an inbound server it accessed while attempting to fulfill the request. This typically happens when an upstream web application crashes or is unreachable.

The 503 Service Unavailable status code indicates that the server is currently unable to handle the request due to a temporary overload or scheduled maintenance. The response should send a Retry-After header indicating how many seconds to back off before retrying.

The WWW-Authenticate response header defines the HTTP authentication method that should be used to gain access to a resource. It is sent along with a 401 Unauthorized response and informs the client of the auth scheme (such as Bearer or Basic) and realm parameters.

The Retry-After response header indicates how long the user agent should wait before making a follow-up request. It can contain either an HTTP-date or a number of seconds in delta-seconds format. It is typically sent with 429 Too Many Requests or 503 Service Unavailable responses.

The Allow header lists the set of methods supported by a resource. It must be provided in a 405 Method Not Allowed response. For example: Allow: GET, POST, HEAD. Clients should check the Allow header to determine which HTTP methods are valid for the given URL path.

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is an HTTP-header based mechanism that allows a server to indicate any origins other than its own from which a browser should permit loading resources. CORS errors are strictly enforced by web browsers. Backend HTTP clients (like curl, Python HTTPX, Axios in Node.js) do not enforce CORS restrictions.

A preflighted CORS request first sends an HTTP request by the OPTIONS method to the resource on the other origin to determine if the actual request is safe to send. The server must reply with Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods, and Access-Control-Allow-Headers headers matching the incoming request.

The Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header indicates whether the response can be shared with requesting code from the given origin. It may specify a wildcard (*) for public APIs or a specific origin. If credentials (cookies/auth) are included, a wildcard cannot be used and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials must be true.

RFC 9110 defines that the 401 (Unauthorized) status code indicates that the request has not been applied because it lacks valid authentication credentials. The origin server generating a 401 response MUST send a WWW-Authenticate header field containing at least one challenge applicable to the target resource.

The 403 (Forbidden) status code indicates that the server understood the request but refuses to fulfill it. An origin server that wishes to make public why the request has been forbidden can describe that reason in the response content. If authentication credentials were provided in the request, the server considers them insufficient to grant access.

The 307 (Temporary Redirect) status code indicates that the target resource resides temporarily under a different URI. The user agent MUST NOT change the request method if it performs an automatic redirection: a POST must remain a POST with the exact same request body. This differs from 302 which historical clients rewrote to GET.

The 405 (Method Not Allowed) status code indicates that the method received in the request-line is known by the origin server but not supported by the target resource. The origin server MUST generate an Allow header field in a 405 response containing a list of the target resource's supported methods.

HTTPX applies granular timeouts across four operations: connect timeout (establishing socket connection), read timeout (waiting for bytes from the server), write timeout (sending request data), and pool timeout (acquiring a connection from the pool). A timeout error is a client-side exception and does not mean the server returned an HTTP status code.

HTTPX raises httpx.ConnectError when a network connection to the target server cannot be established. Common causes include domain name resolution failure (getaddrinfo failed), unreachable hosts, or closed network ports. When DNS resolution fails, no TCP handshake or HTTP request is ever sent.

HTTPX verifies SSL/TLS certificates by default using system trust stores. If the server presents an expired certificate, an untrusted self-signed certificate, or a certificate whose subject name does not match the requested hostname, a ConnectError or ssl.SSLError is raised and the connection is aborted.

By default, HTTPX does not follow HTTP redirects (follow_redirects=False). When the server returns a 301, 302, 307, or 308 response, HTTPX returns the redirect response directly with the target URL in the Location response header. To automatically follow redirects, set follow_redirects=True.

When a request contains invalid data, FastAPI returns an HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity response containing a JSON body with a 'detail' list. Each element in the list contains 'loc' (location of the invalid field in body, query, or path), 'msg' (error description), and 'type' (error type such as missing, int_parsing, or value_error).

In FastAPI and Pydantic models, fields declared without default values are mandatory. If a client sends a JSON body omitting a required field (for example, missing 'title' or 'items'), validation fails immediately with status 422 and error type 'missing'.

FastAPI validates and converts query and body parameters according to Python type annotations. If an integer is expected (e.g. quantity: int) and the client passes a non-numeric string (e.g. 'two'), type conversion fails and FastAPI returns 422 with type int_parsing.

In Axios, the default validateStatus configuration resolves the promise only for HTTP status codes in the 2xx range (status >= 200 && status < 300). Any response with status 4xx or 5xx throws an AxiosError, rejecting the promise. The HTTP response object is accessible via error.response.

Axios allows passing custom headers in the second or third configuration argument. To authenticate with Bearer tokens, pass headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` }. When sending plain JavaScript objects as data, Axios automatically serializes to JSON and sets Content-Type: application/json.

An API endpoint is the specific URL a client calls to reach a resource or operation. It combines a base URL, an optional version prefix, and a resource path, for example https://api.example.com/v1/users/42. The HTTP method is not part of the URL but is part of the operation: GET /users/42 reads the user while DELETE /users/42 removes it. Path parameters such as 42 identify a specific resource and must be URL-encoded. Do not build endpoint URLs by pasting untrusted values together; encode path segments and validate identifiers first.

HTTP methods describe the action. GET reads a resource and should be safe: it must not change server state. POST usually creates a resource or triggers processing and is not automatically idempotent. PUT replaces the entire target resource and is idempotent when the same representation is sent again. PATCH applies a partial modification and may or may not be idempotent depending on the patch format. DELETE removes a resource and is normally idempotent. HEAD returns headers without a body, and OPTIONS reports communication capabilities, including CORS preflight information. A server that knows a method but does not allow it on a resource should return 405 with an Allow header.

An HTTP exchange has a request and a response. A request contains a method, target URL, headers, and an optional body. A response contains a status code, headers, and an optional body. Content-Type describes the media type of the body being sent, while Accept lists the media types the client can read. Authorization carries credentials. The status code summarizes the outcome, and response headers carry metadata such as Location for redirects, Retry-After for rate limits, and ETag for caching. JSON is common for API bodies, but form data, multipart data, XML, and binary payloads are also valid when the Content-Type says so.

Status codes are grouped by their first digit. 1xx means informational and the request is still in progress. 2xx means success, such as 200 OK or 201 Created. 3xx means redirection, such as 301 or 307. 4xx means the client appears to have caused the problem: 400 malformed request, 401 missing or invalid authentication, 403 authenticated but not allowed, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 422 semantic validation failure, 429 rate limited. 5xx means the server failed to fulfill an apparently valid request. Do not retry a 4xx unchanged; fix the request first. Retry 429 and transient 5xx responses with backoff and respect Retry-After.

HTTP headers carry metadata about a request or response. Common request headers include Accept, Content-Type, Authorization, User-Agent, and Idempotency-Key. Common response headers include Content-Type, Location, Retry-After, ETag, Cache-Control, and WWW-Authenticate. Header names are case-insensitive, and a header may appear more than once, so clients and servers should combine repeated values correctly. Use Authorization for credentials rather than putting tokens in the URL, because URLs are frequently written to logs and browser history. Redact sensitive headers before logging or sharing a request.

A URL path identifies the resource: /users/42 means user 42. The query string supplies optional modifiers such as filtering, sorting, searching, or pagination: /users?role=admin&sort=-created_at&limit=20. Path parameters are usually required and identify one resource; query parameters are usually optional and narrow or shape a collection. Encode both with percent-encoding, but never place API keys or session tokens in either. Query parameters are visible in logs and Referer headers. Repeated query keys such as tags=a&tags=b can represent a list; confirm the API's documented convention.

Authentication answers who you are; authorization answers what you are allowed to do. A missing or invalid credential produces 401 Unauthorized and should include a WWW-Authenticate challenge describing the expected scheme. A valid identity that lacks a role, scope, or ownership permission produces 403 Forbidden. Sending the same token again will not fix a 403; inspect scopes, roles, tenant, and resource ownership instead. Logging in again only helps a 401. Protect both layers: verify tokens on the server, enforce authorization on every resource access, and avoid hiding authorization decisions only in the UI.

REST is an architectural style, not a JSON format or a specific library. Its constraints include client-server separation, statelessness, cacheability, a uniform interface, and a layered system. Resources are identified by URLs and manipulated through representations and standard HTTP methods. Statelessness means each request must carry the credentials and context needed to process it; the server does not rely on a previous request. A REST API commonly uses JSON, but JSON alone does not make an API RESTful. Good REST design uses nouns for resources, standard methods for actions, and stable identifiers.

Rate limiting protects a service by capping how many requests a client may make in a time window. A rejected request normally returns 429 Too Many Requests and may include Retry-After plus rate-limit headers showing the limit, remaining count, and reset time. Limits can be enforced per API key, user, IP address, endpoint, or model, and a quota may be a longer-lived allowance separate from a short burst limit. Handle 429 with exponential backoff and jitter, honor Retry-After, and avoid immediate retry loops. Cache responses, batch work, and reduce polling where possible.

Pagination returns large collections in chunks. Offset pagination uses page and per_page or limit and offset; it is easy to understand but becomes slow at deep offsets and can duplicate or skip items when records are inserted or deleted during iteration. Cursor or keyset pagination returns an opaque next_cursor tied to a stable sort key such as created_at plus id; it stays consistent and efficient for large datasets. A good API documents defaults and maximum page sizes, returns a next_cursor or has_next indicator, and keeps a stable ordering. Clients should follow the cursor rather than constructing page numbers themselves.

An idempotent operation can be repeated with the same intended effect. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent by HTTP semantics; POST generally is not, so retrying a POST can create duplicate orders or payments. For unsafe operations, clients can send an Idempotency-Key header containing a unique value per logical operation. The server stores the key together with a request fingerprint and the result, then replays the stored response when the same key is retried. Reuse the same key when retrying after a timeout or connection error, but use a new key for a genuinely new operation.

A webhook is a reverse HTTP callback: a provider sends a POST request to an endpoint you expose when an event occurs. Respond with 2xx quickly, then process the event asynchronously so the provider does not time out. Verify the signature by computing an HMAC over the raw request body with your shared secret and comparing it to the signature header, and reject stale timestamps. Expect at-least-once delivery, duplicates, retries, and out-of-order events, so deduplicate by event ID and make handlers idempotent. Use HTTPS, an allowlist of provider IPs where available, and never trust a webhook solely because it reached your URL.

API versioning lets a provider evolve without breaking existing clients. Common strategies are a path segment such as /v1/users, a custom header, or a media type parameter. Path versioning is easy to see, test, and cache; header or media-type versioning keeps URLs stable but is harder to discover and debug. Prefer additive, backward-compatible changes: add optional fields, never rename or remove fields unexpectedly, and keep default behavior stable. When a version must retire, announce a deprecation window, document a migration path, and signal it with Deprecation and Sunset response headers where appropriate.

source_title: API error responses and Problem Details
chunk_text: A good API error uses the correct HTTP status code and a consistent, machine-readable body. RFC 9457 Problem Details defines fields such as type, title, status, detail, and instance, and allows extension members for validation errors, request IDs, and retry hints. Include a correlation or request ID so support can trace a failure, and list field-level problems for 400 or 422 responses. Never expose stack traces, SQL, secrets, or internal hostnames. Clients should branch on status and error type, not on a human message, and should retry only safe or idempotent requests with backoff.

HTTP caching reduces latency and repeated work. Cache-Control directives such as max-age, s-maxage, no-store, no-cache, private, and public define who may cache a response and for how long. An ETag validator lets a client send If-None-Match; if the representation is unchanged the server replies 304 Not Modified without a body. Last-Modified works with If-Modified-Since as a weaker alternative. Use Vary when the response depends on headers such as Accept or Authorization. Cache safe GET responses, never cache mutations, and mark authenticated responses private unless they are genuinely shareable.

OAuth 2.0 delegates authorization without sharing a user's password. The roles are resource owner, client, authorization server, and resource server. User-facing applications should use Authorization Code with PKCE; machine-to-machine integrations typically use Client Credentials. The client receives a short-lived access token, and optionally a refresh token, then sends the access token in the Authorization header to the resource server. Request the least scopes needed, keep refresh tokens secure and rotate them, and never place tokens in URLs, logs, or frontend source. Always use HTTPS and validate redirect URIs exactly.

A JWT is a compact token with three base64url parts: header, payload, and signature. The payload contains claims such as sub, iss, aud, exp, and nbf. A JWT is signed, not encrypted by default, so anyone holding it can read the payload; never put secrets or sensitive personal data inside. The server must verify the signature with the correct key, then validate issuer, audience, expiry, not-before, and algorithm. Reject the none algorithm and unexpected key types. Use short lifetimes, key rotation, and secure storage. For server-side sessions where revocation matters, an opaque token stored server-side may be simpler.

Use multipart/form-data when a request combines files with other form fields. The body is split into parts by a boundary; each part has a Content-Disposition naming the field and may have its own Content-Type. Let an HTTP client library generate the Content-Type header with the boundary instead of setting it manually, because a mismatched boundary makes the body unparseable. Servers should stream large uploads to temporary storage, enforce size limits, validate the declared and detected media type, sanitize filenames, and never execute uploaded content. For structured data without files, application/json is usually simpler.

To debug an API request, first reproduce it with curl or an HTTP client and confirm the method, URL, path, query, headers, and body. Check that Content-Type matches the actual body and that Authorization uses the documented scheme. Compare the status code with the response body and any request ID. Read the API's error schema and documentation for that exact endpoint and version. Test without optional query parameters, then add them back one at a time. For browser failures, separate CORS or preflight problems from server-side errors by testing the same request outside the browser. Retry only 429 and transient 5xx responses, and log the request ID when contacting support.
